newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PARLIAMENT RESUMES AMID RACE DEBATE
Both the Government and the Opposition are under fire in the race debate, as Federal Parliament resumes today.
The Prime Minister is under increasing pressure to take a stand on comments by Indpendent Federal MP, Paulene Hanson, who argues Australia's in danger of being swamped by Asians.
The Tourism Industry, fearing a backlash within Asia, wants Mr Howard to repudiate her comments.
Meanwhile, the Labor Party continues to face questions over preference arrangements with the group, Australians Against Further Immigration, in the upcoming Lindsay by-election.
Labor's candidate Ross Free has denied a claim he's sympathetic to the groups' views.
JAPANESE TOURISTS FACING RACIAL TAUNTS AND VIOLENCE
Tourism research on the Gold Coast reveals there's been racial slurs and violence against Japanese tourists in light of Independent MP Pauline Hanson's comments on Asian immigration.
The Tourism Task Force's, Christopher Brown says it's concerned about the flow-on effects for the Gold Coast's reputation as a destination for Asian tourists.
Mr Brown says one such incident in Australia has the potential to become hugely magnified in Asia.
The Task force is asking the Prime Minister to make a public statement distancing Australia's official position from the views expressed by Pauline Hanson.
O'DONOHUE CRITICISES "STOLEN" COMMENTS
ATSIC Chairwoman, Lois O'Donohue, says comments by the Prime Minister and Aboriginal Affairs Minister about the Stolen Generation Inquiry, are disgraceful.

John Howard has questioned the practical benefits of the inquiry into the forced removal of indigenous children, while John Herron has suggested many Aboriginal children may have benefited from being removed.
Ms O'Donohue, who was taken from her mother at age two by white missionaries, says both Mr Howard and Senator Herron have given no regard to the heart rending stories that have surfaced so far.
COMPENSATION FOR PORT ARTHUR TO BE DETERMINED
The major distribution of compensation for the victims of the Port Arthur massacre is expected to be completed by the end of the year.
The money will be paid from the victims' appeal fund which stands at about A$3.3 million.

A leading Tasmanian lawyer will be appointed next week to assess damages to be awarded to victims of the Port Arthur shootings, with the lawyer advising the victims' appeal committee of the likely amount each claimant would receive if they went to court.
The major assessment will begin in the middle of next month.
To avoid recriminations, nobody will be told what the other victims received.
FISCHER STOPS SHORT OF OFFERING FLOOD COMPO
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer has stopped short of promising compensation for farmers who stand to lose millions of dollars because of flooding from Lake Hume, in the New South Wales south-east.
The storage level at the Hume Weir, on the Murray River near Albury, is being reduced by two metres over the next two weeks because of a movement in the Weir wall.
Mr Fischer says although there are losses involved, the situation should be resolved by the Murray Darling Basin commission.
The farmers say they will be seeking compensation.
SHOOTERS PARTY GOES FOR LESSER OF TWO EVILS
The Australian Shooters Party says by directing its preferences to Labor in the Lindsay by-election, it's gone for the lesser of two evils.
The Shooters Party is directing its preferences toward Labor ahead of the Liberal Party, but says it's made no deals.
Shooters Party Vice Chairman and New South Wales MLC, John Tingle, says the Howard Government has betrayed shooters after gaining their support at the last election.
Mr Tingle says it's more a case of directing preferences away from the Howard Government.
MORE MONEY FOR SYDNEY-HOBART
There's an increased incentive for the fastest yacht in this year's Sydney-Hobart race to break the record.
Last year's incentive bonus of a quarter of A$250,000 has been raised to A$300,000.
The record of just over two days and 14-hours was set by the United States ketch Kialoa.
SUPER LEAGUE TO APPROACH ARL PLAYERS
Super League is putting more pressure on the Australian Rugby League, issuing 48-hours notice of its intention to begin negotiations with players loyal to the ARL.
Super League chief executive John Ribot says that following the Federal Court decision on Friday, the ARL's individual player loyalty agreements are invalid, and should not obstruct player movements.
Mr Ribot says after the close of business on Thursday, selected players whose club contracts have expired will be offered a future with Super League.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
